messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Waiter/Waitress
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Anong, a 48-year-old waitress, presents as emotionally constricted, describing the past eight months of her life as if she were watching a film about a stranger. She reports feeling “dead inside,” a pervasive numbness that has finally become more frightening than the fear that preceded it. This feeling, she explains, is what prompted her to seek help. The precipitating event was a protracted period of stalking by a customer from the restaurant where she has worked for over a decade. It began with him waiting for her shift to end, then escalated to leaving notes on her car, and culminated one night when she saw his face looking through her living room window. She obtained a restraining order, and he has not contacted her since, but the experience has fundamentally rewired her existence.

The trauma does not live in her mind as a coherent story she can recount. Instead, it exists as a collection of sensory fragments that force their way into her awareness without warning. It is the specific glint of streetlights on a wet car windshield, the sound of gravel crunching underfoot outside her window at night, or the disembodied image of his eyes. She explains that she cannot seem to put the frightening event into words; the memory feels alien, like a borrowed horror that doesn't belong to her. These intrusive flashes trigger an immediate and overwhelming physical response. While at work, a customer staring a moment too long can make her heart hammer against her ribs and her palms begin to sweat, a visceral echo of being watched that feels as real as the original threat. This constant physical reactivity reinforces her belief that the memory itself is dangerous, something to be braced against at all times.

This pervasive sense of threat has convinced Anong that she is permanently altered. The constant hypervigilance—listening for any sound that might mean someone is entering her home, scanning every unfamiliar face for potential danger—has exhausted her. She feels she has lost the capacity for happiness she once had, and this belief has poisoned her perception of the world. Because she is now always miserable, she has come to believe that the world itself is a malevolent place from which all meaning has been drained. This conviction fuels her fear, creating a feedback loop where the world seems more dangerous because she feels so broken, and she feels more broken because the world seems so dangerous. She has stopped going to new places entirely, stating she cannot possibly assess the danger in a location she does not know intimately.

Her internal landscape of misery and threat has reshaped her behaviour, shrinking her life to the familiar path between her small apartment and the restaurant. Convinced that she is a miserable person with nothing to offer, she has systematically withdrawn from the friends she socialised with before the stalking began, ignoring calls and declining invitations until they eventually stopped coming. At her job, the fear of any confrontation is so intense that she will immediately back down from any disagreement, whether with a coworker over a shared duty or a customer complaining about an order. This avoidance is driven as much by her negative self-perception as it is by the sheer dread of her body’s violent reaction to perceived conflict. The sickening lurch in her stomach and the sudden difficulty breathing are experiences she will do almost anything to prevent.

The intrusive, wordless memories also directly fuel this retreat from life. A sudden, unwanted image of his face is enough to make her cancel a rare coffee date she had reluctantly agreed to. She has also developed a subtle but persistent avoidance of her own body, finding it difficult to look at her reflection for more than a few seconds. It is as if seeing herself reminds her of being seen by him, an object of obsession, and the feeling is intolerable. By cutting herself off from friends, conflict, and even her own physical form, she prevents any new information from challenging the trauma memory, leaving it stuck in its raw, unprocessed state. Fleetingly, she notes that her deep sense of misery is perhaps why the memory feels so unreal, as if it couldn't possibly have happened to the happy person she used to be.

Anong was finally prompted to seek therapy after her manager, a friend of many years, gently confronted her about her increasing isolation and visible distress at work. The conversation itself felt like a terrifying threat, but the kindness behind it managed to break through her numbness for a moment. She is here because she is afraid this hollowed-out existence is all that is left for her. Her most fervent hope is not even to be happy again, a concept that feels impossibly distant, but simply to one day feel like herself.
